patient_information: A 20-year-old woman from a rural area of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, mother of three children, with no relevant past medical history.
chief_complaint: Fever, malaise, headache, dry cough, swelling of the neck, and a disseminated skin rash.
history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 2 days prior to the rash. The skin lesions first appeared on the face, then spread centrifugally over her body, including the palms, soles of her feet, and oral mucosa. The lesions evolved from macules to papules, then to vesicles, and finally to pustules. Oral mucosal lesions were painful, making drinking and eating difficult.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient resides in a village in a rural area of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where people live from agriculture. She was born after the worldwide smallpox vaccination programs were stopped in the early 1980s.
vitals: Temperature 38°C (100.4°F), pulse 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 105/82 mmHg.
physical_exam: Disseminated uniform umbilicated vesiculopustular skin lesions (0.5 to 1 cm) all over the body, with a predilection for the face, hands, and feet. Generalized lymphadenopathy with prominent swelling of the cervical lymph nodes. Lungs, heart, abdomen, and CNS examination were unremarkable.
labs_and_diagnostics: WBC 4.4 x 10^9/L (neutrophils: 73%, lymphocytes: 21%), Haemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, ESR 75 mm/h. Definitive diagnosis can be established by PCR, culture, immunohistochemistry, or electron microscopy requiring biosafety level 2 facilities, with optimal specimens being lesion exudate or crust.
management_and_clinical_course: Clinical management was exclusively supportive as no specific vaccine or treatment was available. The patient made an uneventful recovery with scarring from the skin lesions.
